scenes.heading: Copy a good plant. Then conditions change.

voiceover.text: Imagine you've grown a strawberry plant with the fruit you want. You can make new plants from it, so why start again with an uncertain result? Copying sounds useful. Then a new disease reaches the farm. Could those copies share a weakness as well as the fruit characteristics you wanted? To answer that, we need to follow what a new plant inherits.

scenes.heading: A new plant can become a new parent.

voiceover.text: First, a plant growing more leaves is still the same individual. Reproduction makes another individual: an offspring. Here, the small plant has its own roots and leaves. Once established, it can grow separately, and later it can make offspring too. The original plant will not live for ever, but another generation can follow it. The new plant also receives DNA from its parent. DNA carries inherited information, information passed from parent to offspring, that helps shape the plant's characteristics. For the population to continue, enough offspring must survive and reproduce in turn.

scenes.heading: A runner keeps a useful inherited combination.

voiceover.text: The connecting stem is a runner. A new plant grows from it without a sperm cell and an egg cell joining. We call that asexual reproduction. As the new cells form, they copy the parent's DNA. The daughter usually has almost the same inherited information as its parent, so we call it a clone. That's why runners are useful to our grower: they can keep a valued inherited combination instead of mixing it with information from another plant. Similar DNA does not mean every plant grows exactly alike, because growing conditions still matter.

scenes.heading: Sperm and egg join in sexual reproduction.

voiceover.text: A strawberry plant can also make offspring through a flower. Consider a cross between two genetically different plants, meaning their inherited DNA differs. Inside a flower of one parent, a sperm cell from the other joins an egg cell. Sperm and egg are reproductive cells called gametes. Each contributes DNA. Reproduction in which gametes join is called sexual reproduction. The developing new plant is inside a seed, and that seed can grow into a seedling. So the runner and this cross both produce new plants, but the cross brings inherited information from the two parents together.

Move next to a botanically correct seed context and recognisable young strawberry seedling. The intermediate route by which sperm reaches egg is intentionally not animated here.

voiceover.text: How can the same two parents produce different seedlings? Different sperm cells can carry different selections of one parent's inherited information. Egg cells can differ in the same way. When different pairs join, the seedlings can receive different combinations of DNA. Those differences in inherited information are genetic variation. Here is the contrast we need: runner offspring usually retain the parent's combination, while offspring from this cross can inherit different combinations. That gives the grower different plants to compare. It does not tell us which one will perform best.

scenes.heading: A useful copy can share a weakness.

voiceover.text: Now return to the disease at the farm. The grower copied a plant because its inherited characteristics were useful. But if that plant also has an inherited weakness against the new disease, its clones may share it. That is a shared risk, not proof that every plant will become infected. Seedlings with different inherited combinations may respond differently, if the parents carry differences that matter for this disease. Copying helps keep a combination we already value. Sexual reproduction can offer different combinations to compare when conditions change. For this grower, a useful reminder is: copy to keep, cross to compare. The choice still depends on the conditions and the purpose.

scenes.heading: Different combinations give a wider search.

voiceover.text: The crossed seedlings are the better starting group for a search for different inherited responses. They receive DNA through sexual reproduction from genetically different parents, so they can inherit different combinations. Runner offspring usually copy a much narrower set of inherited information from one parent. But we still cannot predict which seedling will grow well in the dry soil. The parents may not carry useful differences for that condition, and a particular seedling may not receive a useful combination. We would need to compare how the plants actually grow there. More variation gives us possibilities to investigate, not a promised winner.

voiceover.text: Reproduction provides new individuals and passes inherited information to another generation. Copying can keep a useful combination; sexual reproduction can produce different inherited combinations. Neither route guarantees that offspring will survive. Next, we'll look at how different animals bring sperm and egg together and support the development of their offspring. The detailed plant mechanisms follow in their own lessons.

points: Reproduction produces offspring and passes on DNA. Enough offspring must survive and reproduce for a population to continue.
Asexual reproduction occurs without gametes joining. Runner offspring usually retain the parent's inherited combination.
Sexual reproduction joins gametes and can produce different inherited combinations. Useful differences depend on the conditions.
